{"source": {"id": "MLP-336", "title": "Myasthenia Gravis", "url": "https://medlineplus.gov/myastheniagravis.html", "content": "What is myasthenia gravis? Myasthenia gravis, sometimes called MG, is a chronic (long-lasting) disease that causes weakness in your voluntary muscles. The voluntary muscles are the ones that you can control. They include the muscles you use for: Eye and eyelid movement Facial expressions Chewing Talking Swallowing Breathing Moving your arms and legs You can also have weakness in other muscles. This weakness gets worse with activity, and better with rest. Myasthenia gravis is a type of autoimmune disease. In autoimmune diseases , your immune system attacks the healthy cells of your organs and tissues by mistake. What causes myasthenia gravis? Myasthenia gravis is caused by an error in how nerve signals are sent to muscles. These signals get blocked at the nerve-muscle junction. This junction is the place where the nerve endings connect with the muscles they control. Normally, this is how the signals work: The signals travel down a nerve that controls movement in the muscle The nerve endings release a substance called acetylcholine Acetylcholine binds to the muscle tissue at the nerve-muscle junction This causes the muscle to contract (move) But in someone with myasthenia gravis, the body's own immune system makes antibodies that block the binding of acetylcholine to the muscle. This makes the muscles weaker. The thymus gland, which is part of your immune system, may play a role in myasthenia gravis. Normally, your thymus gland is active and growing when you are a child. It makes white blood cells to fight infections. At puberty, it starts getting smaller and is replaced by fat. It is usually small by the time you are an adult. But in many adults with myasthenia gravis, the thymus gland stays large. And some people with myasthenia gravis can get thymomas, which are tumors of the thymus. The are usually benign (not cancer), but they can sometimes become cancerous . Who is more likely to develop myasthenia gravis? Although myasthenia gravis can affect people of any age, it is most common in young adult women (under age 40) and older men (over age 60). It is usually not inherited (passed down in families). Myasthenia gravis normally does not affect infants. But if you are pregnant and have myasthenia gravis it's possible to pass the antibodies to your fetus. The baby can then be born with neonatal myasthenia. This condition is usually temporary, and the symptoms typically go away within two to three months after birth. What are the symptoms of myasthenia gravis? The symptoms of myasthenia gravis will depend on which muscles are affected. The symptoms often include: Weakness of the eye muscles Drooping of one or both eyelids Blurred or double vision Changes in facial expressions Trouble swallowing Shortness of breath Speech problems Weakness in the arms, hands, fingers, legs, and neck Different people have different levels of muscle weakness. And the weakness can vary from day to day. Some days it might be mild, and other days it might be worse. Physical activity often makes the muscle weakness worse. Some people with myasthenia gravis can get severe weakness that affects the muscles that control breathing. This is called a myasthenic crisis, and it is a life-threatening emergency. How is myasthenia gravis diagnosed? There are many other conditions that can cause muscle weakness, so myasthenia gravis can be hard to diagnose. To find out if you have myasthenia gravis, your health care provider: Will ask about your medical history and symptoms Will do a physical exam, including a neurological exam Will likely order tests for myasthenia gravis , including: Blood tests Imaging tests Electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction studies What are the treatments for myasthenia gravis? There is no cure for myasthenia gravis, but treatments that can improve muscle weakness and help with symptoms. They include: Anticholinesterase medicines, which can improve nerve-to-muscle messages and make muscles stronger. Immunosuppressive medicines, which are medicines that decrease your body's immune system responses. They can lower your body's production of abnormal antibodies. Monoclonal antibodies, which can also help decrease your body's immune system responses. Plasmapheresis (plasma exchange) and intravenous immunoglobulin, which are procedures to remove abnormal antibodies from your blood. They are usually used in severe cases. They can help with symptoms for a few weeks or months. Thymectomy, surgery to remove the thymus gland. It can reduce the symptoms of myasthenia gravis, possibly by rebalancing the immune system. Lifestyle changes may be helpful for some people. The changes could include regular gentle exercise, getting enough rest, and eating healthy foods. Some people with myasthenia gravis go into remission. This means that they do not have symptoms. The remission is usually temporary, but sometimes it can be permanent. NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke", "groups": ["Brain and Nerves"], "source": "MedlinePlus, National Library of Medicine", "language": "en"}, "candidate": {"positive_en": "In myasthenia gravis or MG, what role do acetylcholine and antibodies play at the nerve-muscle junction?", "positive_zh": "在重症肌无力MG中，乙酰胆碱和抗体在神经肌肉接头处起什么作用？", "evidence": "Acetylcholine binds to the muscle tissue at the nerve-muscle junction This causes the muscle to contract (move) But in someone with myasthenia gravis, the body's own immune system makes antibodies that block the binding of acetylcholine to the muscle. This makes the muscles weaker.", "expected_answer": "Normally, acetylcholine binds to muscle tissue at the nerve-muscle junction and causes contraction; in myasthenia gravis, antibodies block acetylcholine binding, making muscles weaker.", "missing_en": "What exact percentage of people with MG achieve permanent remission after thymectomy?", "missing_reason": "The summary does not provide a permanent remission percentage after thymectomy. It only says thymectomy can reduce symptoms, possibly by rebalancing the immune system, and that remission is usually temporary but sometimes permanent."}}

The positive_zh translation asks the exact same question about acetylcholine and antibodies at the nerve-muscle junction. The missing_en question asks for a specific percentage of permanent remission after thymectomy, which is a meaningful on-topic detail - the source only states thymectomy can reduce symptoms and that remission 'sometimes can be permanent' without providing any percentage figures."}

The source summary provides information about myasthenia gravis, including:
- What MG is (autoimmune disease causing weakness in voluntary muscles)
- The mechanism involving acetylcholine at the nerve-muscle junction
- The role of antibodies blocking acetylcholine binding
- Various treatments including thymectomy

**positive_supported**:

The evidence provided shows: "Acetylcholine binds to the muscle tissue at the nerve-muscle junction This causes the muscle to contract (move) But in someone with myasthenia gravis, the body's own immune system makes antibodies that block the binding of acetylcholine to the muscle. This makes the muscles weaker."

This directly and fully answers the positive_en question. The expected_answer matches exactly what the evidence states. So positive_supported = true.

**translation_equivalent**:
positive_zh asks: "在重症肌无力MG中，乙酰胆碱和抗体在神经肌肉接头处起什么作用？"
This is asking the same thing as positive_en - the role of acetylcholine and antibodies at the nerve-muscle junction. The source provides the answer. So translation_equivalent = true (because it asks the same thing without supplying the answer - that's what the task is asking about).

**missing_absent**:
missing_en asks: "What exact percentage of people with MG achieve permanent remission after thymectomy?"
The source says: "Thymectomy, surgery to remove the thymus gland. It can reduce the symptoms of myasthenia gravis, possibly by rebalancing the immune system." and "Some people with myasthenia gravis go into remission. This means that they do not have symptoms. The remission is usually temporary, but sometimes it can be permanent."


The source does not provide any specific percentage about permanent remission after thymectomy. This is a meaningful on-topic detail not stated in the source. So missing_absent = true.

The analysis reveals multiple critical points: the question about acetylcholine and antibodies is fully addressed, the Chinese translation maintains the same inquiry, and the source lacks precise statistical information about permanent remission rates following thymectomy. The evidence comprehensively supports the understanding of myasthenia gravis's underlying mechanisms, particularly at the neuromuscular junction.
